files.lesson.md: --- order: 8 unit: circles node: AC9M7M03 n3 uses: [AC9M7N06 n2, AC9M7A03 n2] # dividing decimals; undoing an operation (backtracking: d = C ÷ π) title: Circumference summary: "Because C ÷ d = π, the circumference is π × diameter: C = πd, or C = 2πr from the radius. Going backwards, d = C ÷ π." language: maths voice: { name: af_heart, speed: 1.1 } hook: "A bike wheel 70 cm across rolls forward one circumference with every turn. How many turns to school? A trundle wheel measures a sports field the same way." connection: bike-computer app: command: node "$REPO_ROOT/tools/serve.mjs" "$REPO_ROOT/dist/_playground-board" 8280 url: http://127.0.0.1:8280/index.html readySelector: "#sl-r" layout: full explainPicture: { ref: circle.yml#explain-pic, caption: "Radius 2.5 cm, diameter 5 cm: rolled out, $C = \\pi \\times 5 \\approx 15.71$ cm." } explainClip: query: { code: "@circle.yml#explain", fresh: 1, id: explain } caption: "C = πd" say: "The circumference is pi times the diameter." clip: - caption: { text: "Radius 2, diameter 4: C = π × 4 ≈ 12.57.", say: "Diameter four: the circumference is pi times four." } - wait: 1400 - caption: { text: "Double the radius: the circumference doubles too.", say: "Double the radius, and the circumference doubles too." } - click: Make the radius bigger - click: Make the radius bigger - expect: { selector: "#gsum", contains: "circumference 25.13" } - wait: 1400 --- The last lesson found that $C \div d = \pi$ for every circle. Use $\pi \approx 3.14$, as the questions say. ## Predict: radius 5 ```step stage: predict insight: "Committing to a circumference for radius 5 shows whether they double to the diameter first, or use the radius as if it were the diameter." check: type: predict q: "A circle has radius 5 cm. About how long is its circumference?" options: ["31.4 cm", "15.7 cm", "78.5 cm", "10 cm"] actual: "31.4 cm. The diameter is 10 cm, and π × 10 ≈ 31.4. 15.7 uses the radius as the diameter; 10 cm is the diameter itself." ``` Find the diameter first. ## Run: roll radius 2.5 ```step stage: run insight: "Rolling a circle of a given radius checks C = πd = 2πr against the track it leaves." try: { playground: board, starter: "circle.yml#run", height: 640 } check: { type: board, text: "Make a circle with radius 2.5 cm and roll it out. Work out π × d first, then compare. Was your prediction method right?", when: "r = 2.5 and o = 1", explain: "d = 5 cm, so C = π × 5 ≈ 15.71 cm." } ``` Predict the circumference from the diameter before you roll. Here's the rule behind the roll. Turned round, $C \div d = \pi$ gives a formula for the circumference: $$C = \pi d \qquad \text{or, since } d = 2r, \qquad C = 2\pi r$$ Going backwards, from a circumference to the diameter, divide by π: $d = C \div \pi$. ## Investigate: forwards and backwards ```step stage: investigate insight: "C = πd uses the diameter (Mei uses the radius instead); C = 2πr is the same rule. Going backwards divides by π; students own the working and pick the key reason." tasks: - check: type: answer q: "A circle has diameter 8 cm. Using π ≈ 3.14, what is its circumference, in cm?" answer: "25.12" feedback: - ["12.56", "That uses half the diameter. C = π × d = 3.14 × 8."] - ["50.24", "That uses 16, twice the diameter."] explain: "3.14 × 8 = 25.12 cm." - check: type: bug code: "working.txt#mei" text: "Mei finds how far a wheel rolls in one turn. Click the line where her working goes wrong." answer: 3 fault: logic misconception: radius-diameter explain: "Line 3: 30 cm is the radius, but C = π × d needs the diameter, 60 cm. 3.14 × 60 = 188.4 cm (or C = 2πr = 2 × 3.14 × 30)." - check: type: reasoning q: "A circular garden bed has circumference 18.84 m. Using π ≈ 3.14, find its diameter. Write your steps." steps: - ["$C = \\pi d$, so $18.84 = 3.14 \\times d$", "the circumference is π times the diameter"] - ["$d = 18.84 \\div 3.14 = 6$ m", "divide by π to undo multiplying by π"] picks: - step: 2 options: ["Divide by π to undo multiplying by π", "Multiply by π again", "Divide by 2, because d = 2r"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "That gives 59.2 m, bigger than the circumference. A diameter is always shorter: divide.", "Halving gives a radius from a diameter, not a diameter from a circumference."] answer: "6" feedback: - ["59.1576", "That multiplies by π. Divide instead."] - ["3", "That is the radius. The question asks for the diameter."] explain: "18.84 ÷ 3.14 = 6 m." ``` ### Use the diameter Here is the formula forwards and backwards. ```worked C = \pi d = 3.14 \times 8 = 25.12 \text{ cm} :: From the diameter: multiply by π. C = 2\pi r = 2 \times 3.14 \times 30 = 188.4 \text{ cm} :: From the radius: double it first (2r is the diameter). d = C \div \pi = 18.84 \div 3.14 = 6 \text{ m} :: Backwards: divide by π. C = 10\pi \text{ cm} :: Exact: leave π in the answer (for d = 10). 10π means 10 × π, about 31.4. ``` Now try one: diameter 8 cm. ### Find the mistake Read Mei's working. Which length does C = πd need? ### Backwards Your working can be short notes. Then choose the reason for the key step. ## Modify: one change at a time ```step stage: modify insight: "One change at a time: building a circumference on the board, using 22/7, an exact answer, a radius from a circumference (two steps), then a semicircle's perimeter." try: { playground: board, starter: "circle.yml#twentyfive", height: 640 } tasks: - starter: "circle.yml#twentyfive" hint: ["25 ÷ 3.14 is about 8: that is the diameter.", "Radius 4."] check: { type: board, text: "Make and roll a circle with circumference about 25 cm (between 24.5 and 25.5).", when: "c > 24.5 and c < 25.5 and o = 1", explain: "d = 8 cm (r = 4): C = π × 8 ≈ 25.13 cm." } - check: type: answer q: "Using π ≈ 22/7, find the circumference of a circle with radius 7 cm." answer: "44" feedback: - ["22", "That uses the radius as the diameter. d = 14."] explain: "C = 2 × 22/7 × 7 = 44 cm." - check: type: question q: "What is the exact circumference of a circle with diameter 6 cm?" options: ["$6\\pi$ cm", "$3\\pi$ cm", "$12\\pi$ cm", "$6 + \\pi$ cm"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "3 is the radius. C = π × d.", "12 is twice the diameter.", "C is π times d, not π added."] explain: "C = π × 6 = 6π cm (about 18.84 cm)." - check: type: answer q: "A circle has circumference 31.4 cm. Using π ≈ 3.14, what is its radius, in cm?" answer: "5" feedback: - ["10", "That is the diameter. Halve it for the radius."] explain: "d = 31.4 ÷ 3.14 = 10 cm, so r = 5 cm." - check: type: question q: "Edge case: a semicircle has diameter 10 cm. What is its perimeter (the curved edge and the straight edge)? Use π ≈ 3.14." options: ["25.7 cm", "15.7 cm", "31.4 cm", "41.4 cm"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "That is only the curved edge. Add the straight diameter.", "That is a whole circle's circumference.", "Half of the circle's circumference, not all of it, plus 10."] explain: "Half of 31.4 is 15.7, plus the 10 cm diameter: 25.7 cm." ``` ### Circumference 25 Each task changes one thing. ### With 22/7 ### Exact ### Backwards: the radius ### A semicircle ## Practise: circumference ```step stage: practise insight: "Forwards from d and r, a real-world distance and a review, mixed; using the radius as the diameter is the planted slip." tasks: - check: type: answer q: "Diameter 12 cm. Circumference, in cm (π ≈ 3.14)?" answer: "37.68" feedback: - ["18.84", "12 is the diameter already: do not halve it."] explain: "3.14 × 12 = 37.68 cm." - check: type: answer q: "Radius 3 cm. Circumference, in cm (π ≈ 3.14)?" answer: "18.84" feedback: - ["9.42", "That uses the radius as the diameter. d = 6."] explain: "2 × 3.14 × 3 = 18.84 cm." - check: type: answer q: "A bike wheel has diameter 70 cm. How far does the bike go in 100 turns, in metres (π ≈ 3.14)?" answer: "219.8" feedback: - ["21980", "That is in centimetres. 100 cm = 1 m."] - ["109.9", "70 cm is the diameter: do not halve it."] explain: "One turn: 3.14 × 70 = 219.8 cm. 100 turns: 21 980 cm = 219.8 m." - check: type: answer q: "Review: a triangle has base 10 cm and height 6 cm. Its area, in cm²?" answer: "30" feedback: - ["60", "Halve it."] explain: "½ × 10 × 6 = 30 cm²." ``` ### From the diameter ### From the radius ### A bike ride ### Review: area ## Make: a trundle wheel ```step stage: make insight: "Designing a trundle wheel that clicks every metre turns C = πd round: the diameter is 100 ÷ π, a real design problem with a sensible rounding." hint: ["One turn should roll exactly 1 m = 100 cm.", "C = πd, so d = 100 ÷ 3.14."] check: type: number q: "A trundle wheel clicks once each turn. What diameter, in cm to one decimal place, makes it click once every metre? (π ≈ 3.14)" answer: 31.8 tolerance: 0.15 explain: "One turn is the circumference: 100 cm. d = 100 ÷ 3.14 ≈ 31.8 cm (radius about 15.9 cm)." ``` Then work out how many clicks it makes around a 400 m running track. ## Make: set the bike computer, on paper ```step stage: make insight: "A bike computer needs the distance one turn rolls, which is the circumference; the wheel is given across, so the diameter goes straight into C = πd with no halving or doubling." hint: ["Is 700 mm the radius or the diameter?", "Multiply the diameter by 3.14."] check: type: reasoning paper: true q: "A bike computer asks for the wheel's circumference in mm when you set it up. The wheel is 700 mm across. Using π ≈ 3.14, what do you type in? Give the nearest whole number of millimetres." steps: - ["The wheel is 700 mm across, so $d = 700$ mm", "across means the diameter"] - ["$C = \\pi d = 3.14 \\times 700$", "the circumference is π times the diameter"] - ["$C = 2198$ mm", "about 2.2 m for every turn"] picks: - step: 2 q: "Which length do you multiply by π?" options: - "The diameter, the width across: 700" - "The radius: 350" - "The diameter squared" answer: 0 feedback: [null, "With the radius you need a 2 as well (C = 2πr). 3.14 × 350 is only half the way round.", "Squaring is for area. The circumference is a length."] answer: "2198" tolerance: 2 feedback: - ["1099", "That uses 350, half of 700. The 700 mm is already the diameter."] - ["4396", "That doubles the diameter. C = π × d needs no extra 2."] criteria: - "I said whether 700 mm is the radius or the diameter." - "I multiplied that length by 3.14." - "My answer is in millimetres and is a bit over 3 times 700." explain: "d = 700 mm, so C = 3.14 × 700 = 2198 mm." ``` Do this one in your book, not on the screen. Real tyres squash a little under a rider, so a rider rolls the bike one turn along chalk and measures. Write which length you have, multiply, check it is a bit over 3 diameters, and type the millimetres. **Also used in** - **Racing.** In a 400 m race the outer lanes start further forward, because each lane's bends make a bigger circle. - **Rolling wheels.** A wheel rolled one turn along the ground travels one circumference, which is how C ÷ d was first found. - **Trundle wheels.** A wheel that clicks once a turn measures a field, if its circumference is a metre. ```teacher summary: Students use C = πd and C = 2πr to find circumferences, check against circles rolled out on the board, go backwards with d = C ÷ π, and design a trundle wheel (AC9M7M03, node 3). time: 45 timing: Predict and Run 8 min · Investigate 15 min · Modify 12 min · Practise and Make 10 min goals: - I can find a circle's circumference from its diameter or radius. - I can find a diameter or radius from a circumference. - I can give an exact answer in terms of π. struggle: Going backwards from a circumference to a radius takes two steps (divide by π, then halve). Ask students to write which length they have and which they want before they press any calculator keys. before: > Do the Run board yourself first. Students need π as C ÷ d (previous lesson), d = 2r, and dividing decimals (a calculator is fine). The one idea: C = πd, because that is what π means. The common mistake is using the radius in place of the diameter (Mei's mistake, a spiral of Parts of a circle). Rearranging to d = C ÷ π uses the inverse-operations idea from Algebra. running: - "Predict: students who chose 15.7 used the radius as the diameter." - "Run: ask students to predict before rolling, then compare." - "Investigate: share two routes for the wheel: C = π × 60, or C = 2 × π × 30." - "Modify: for the semicircle, ask students to trace the whole outline with a finger." - "Make: build a cardboard trundle wheel if there is time." - "Paper: the bike computer is worked in books; the page marks the millimetres and the reason for using the diameter, then shows a model. Books out, and look for 'diameter' written next to 700." stuck: - see: A student multiplies π by the radius (Mei's mistake). ask: Is the given length across the whole circle or half way? fix: Double the radius to get the diameter, or use C = 2πr. - see: A student multiplies by π when going backwards. ask: Should the diameter be bigger or smaller than the circumference? fix: "Smaller: divide by π." - see: A student forgets units or mixes cm and m. ask: What unit is your answer in? What does the question want? fix: "Convert at the end: 100 cm = 1 m." stretch: The Earth's equator is about 40 000 km. Estimate the Earth's diameter. If a rope round the equator were made 1 m longer, how high above the ground would it float? support: Keep C = πd and d = 2r on the board; use 3.14 on a calculator (the π key gives answers a little different from 3.14). leads: > This completes AC9M7M03. Where it leads: the area of a circle and composite shapes with circles (Year 8), arc length (Year 10), and Pythagoras (AC9M8M06, next in this pathway). exit: q: "Find the circumference of a circle with radius 4 cm. A circle has circumference 12.56 cm: find its diameter. (π ≈ 3.14)" a: 2 × 3.14 × 4 = 25.12 cm. 12.56 ÷ 3.14 = 4 cm. explain: > Because $C \div d = \pi$, the circumference is $$C = \pi d = 2\pi r$$ Use the diameter (or double the radius). Going backwards, divide by π: $d = C \div \pi$. An exact answer keeps π: a circle with diameter 10 cm has $C = 10\pi$ cm, about 31.4 cm. ```
